summary: Analyzes how enterprise networks, which have multiple internal links and connections to one or more providers, can move to IPv6, focusing on the IP layer. It identifies transition scenarios and requirements that build on an earlier document about enterprise scenarios. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A company with many rooms and doors to the outside has to switch to a new kind of address. This paper looks at the problems that come up while the company changes over.

questions: how do enterprises transition to ipv6
subtitle: Analyzing how organizations can transition to IPv6 while running both IPv4 and IPv6 on their networks.

tldr.problem: Enterprise networks with multiple internal links and external provider connections need guidance on transitioning to IPv6 while maintaining IPv4. The challenges differ depending on the network's size, structure, and whether providers support IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes different enterprise network topologies and provides a staged deployment strategy. It examines when to use dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6 together), when to tunnel IPv6 over IPv4, and when to build parallel infrastructure, with specific recommendations for each scenario.
tldr.outcome: Enterprises can use this analysis to plan IPv6 adoption incrementally, starting with external connectivity and DNS, then deploying IPv6 more widely while continuing to run IPv4 where needed.

today: RFC 4852 remains an Informational RFC relevant to enterprises planning IPv6 adoption. While published in 2007, the fundamental challenges and staged deployment approach remain applicable. Many enterprises have followed similar strategies to those described in this document as they have gradually transitioned toward IPv6-primary networks.

sections.title: Enterprise IPv6 Transition
sections.content:
RFC 4852 analyzes IPv6 adoption in enterprise networks, focusing on the IP layer. Enterprise networks are large internal networks with multiple links and connections to one or more external providers, managed by a network operations team. This document builds on earlier work about enterprise scenarios and provides detailed transition analysis assuming enterprises will run dual-stack networks: both IPv4 and IPv6 on the same routers and hosts during the transition period.

The RFC is aimed at enterprise network teams planning IPv6 deployment, including managers, network operations staff, and engineers. It presents notional network models (simplified examples) and provides specific transition mechanism recommendations for each model. The document focuses only on the IP Layer 3 and does not address Layer 4 transport protocols, application porting, VPN security, network management, QoS, or novel IPv6 services like Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: Big companies have networks with lots of computers. They need to switch from old-style network addresses to new ones, but they can't turn everything off at once. This explains how to plan the switch.

sections.title: Enterprise Network Models and Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a matrix tool to categorize different combinations of IPv4 and IPv6 deployment across enterprise networks and external providers. It then covers three main deployment scenarios. Wide-Scale Dual-Stack is when most of the enterprise network supports both IPv4 and IPv6. This can be done in stages: first enable dual-stack on existing routers and hosts, then add new IPv6 routing capability. If internal routers cannot support IPv6, enterprises can tunnel IPv6 over the existing IPv4 infrastructure or build a parallel IPv6 network.

Sparse Dual-Stack Deployment occurs when only some locations or departments run IPv6 while the rest remain IPv4-only. In this case, the enterprise must decide whether to tunnel IPv6 from inside the network to external providers or tunnel from edge routers. Manual configuration and autoconfiguration are both viable depending on the scenario.

IPv6-Dominant Networks are discussed for cases where IPv6 becomes the primary protocol, though this is still uncommon. The RFC also presents a crisis management network scenario in the appendix, showing a realistic example of how an enterprise with varied requirements across departments can deploy IPv6.
sections.eli5: Companies can switch in different ways: everyone at once, just some offices, or gradually. Each way has tradeoffs between cost and how quickly you're done.

sections.title: Network Infrastructure and Transition Stages
sections.content:
The RFC identifies key infrastructure requirements for successful IPv6 transition. Enterprises must obtain external IPv6 connectivity and a globally unique IPv6 address space. They must plan their internal IPv6 addressing carefully, considering aggregation and routing efficiency. DNS must support both A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6), and DNS servers themselves must be IPv6-capable to resolve queries from IPv6-only sources.

The RFC recommends a three-stage deployment approach. Stage 1 establishes external IPv6 connectivity and acquires a global IPv6 address block. Stage 2 involves deploying basic IPv6 infrastructure: an addressing plan, DNS with IPv6 support, IPv6 routing, host configuration, and security controls. Stage 3 consists of widespread dual-stack deployment across internal networks, operating both protocols in parallel.

Throughout the transition, enterprises must address network security, ensuring firewalls and intrusion detection work with IPv6, and selecting appropriate transition mechanisms for each part of the network.
sections.eli5: To switch addresses, you need: new addresses from your Internet company, a plan for numbering your computers, working DNS so computers can find each other, and security rules that work with the new addresses.

sections.title: Transition Mechanisms and Address Handling
sections.content:
Several transition mechanisms are available depending on network readiness. Dual-stack is the simplest when both IPv4 and IPv6 are supported end-to-end. When IPv6-capable devices need to communicate but some infrastructure in between supports only IPv4, tunneling encapsulates IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets. Address translation mechanisms like NAT64 can translate between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, though the RFC notes this has limitations.

The RFC emphasizes that enterprise addressing realms may overlap with provider addressing realms, and customer addressing schemes may conflict. Address mapping and translation mechanisms are needed to handle these scenarios. The document identifies incompatible network touchpoints (where IPv6-only devices cannot reach IPv4-only services) and application incompatibilities (where applications rely on IPv4 features).

The key insight is that different parts of the network may need different mechanisms. A provider might support IPv6 in one region but not another. An enterprise datacenter might be IPv6-ready while branch offices are not. The RFC recommends using multiple mechanisms in combination to support a smooth transition strategy.
sections.eli5: You can keep old and new addresses working at the same time, wrap new addresses in old ones to send them through old-only parts of the network, or translate between them like a phone interpreter.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Deploying IPv6 in enterprise networks requires security controls at every transition stage. IPv6-aware firewalls must be deployed before opening external IPv6 connectivity. Network monitoring and intrusion detection systems must understand IPv6 traffic patterns. Access control lists and security policies must be updated for both protocols. The RFC recommends that enterprises avoid exposing internal network structure through IPv6 addressing and ensure that security zones defined for IPv4 are mirrored in the IPv6 network.

From an operational perspective, enterprises must train network operations staff on IPv6, update monitoring and management systems, and plan carefully for coexistence scenarios. The document notes that dual-stack deployment is not a final state but a transition: at some point, either IPv4 or IPv6 becomes dominant, and resources can be consolidated. Until then, the overhead of supporting both protocols must be managed.
sections.eli5: When you add a new address system, you need new security rules, new ways to monitor the network, and staff who understand both systems.

sections.title: Practical Recommendations and Applicability
sections.content:
The RFC provides specific transition mechanism recommendations for each notational network model. For wide-scale dual-stack scenarios, enterprises should prioritize getting IPv6 routing working, then deploying dual-stack hosts. For sparse deployments, tunnel endpoints at the network edge are preferred because they concentrate IPv6-related complexity in one place. The document emphasizes starting with external connectivity and expanding inward.

Key takeaway recommendations include: obtain external IPv6 connectivity early, develop a comprehensive IPv6 addressing plan before deploying, enable IPv6 on DNS infrastructure first, deploy IPv6 routing before enabling IPv6 on hosts, carefully manage transition mechanism deployment, and coordinate with external providers on their IPv6 support. The RFC notes that the specific strategy depends on the enterprise's current infrastructure, provider support, and business priorities. Not all enterprises will follow the same path or timeline.
sections.eli5: Start by getting a new address from your Internet company and making sure you can talk to them with the new addresses. Then add new addresses to your computers and servers, being careful to keep the old system working the whole time.
